html:
The Tadrart Acacus is a range of rocky hills in the Sahara of southwest Libya, where thousands of paintings and engravings were made from about 12,000 BCE to the first century CE.

The art records the changes of the Sahara. The oldest images show giraffes, elephants and crocodiles from a time when the desert was green. Later come herds of cattle and their herders, then horses and chariots, and last camels, as the land dried out.

The site became a World Heritage Site in 1985. It is threatened by vandalism and oil exploration. Together with Tassili n'Ajjer across the border in Algeria, it is one of the great rock art regions of the world. See also the Garamantes and the Saharan herders.
sum: The Tadrart Acacus is a range of rocky hills in the Sahara of southwest Libya, where thousands of paintings and engravings were made from about 12,000 BCE to the first century CE.
